newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore PM unassailable after election landslide.
newsitem.headline: Singapore PM unassailable after election landslide.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong savoured victory on Friday after his party's best general election result for 16 years.
Goh, whose People's Action Party (PAP) won 65 percent of the vote and all but two seats, had staked his prestige on keeping the opposition presence in parliament to a minimum.

"This is a watershed election," Goh told a news conference, adding voters had "rejected Western-style liberal democracy and freedoms, putting individual rights over that of society" which he said had been "promoted by the Western media".

"This is a magnificent triumph for Goh," said Narayan Ganesan, senior lecturer in Southeast Asian affairs at the National University of Singapore. "As leader of the team, Goh can claim the prize for winning -- unquestioned authority."

The PAP won the election before a single vote was cast when opposition parties decided to contest only 36 seats in the 83-member parliament. The opposition hoped concentrating on few seats would give them a better chance of winning representation.
Opposition parties held four seats in the previous assembly.

But Goh said at the start of the nine-day election campaign he did not want any opposition members in parliament disrupting the progress of a country his party has helped make rich through a paternalistic pro-business policy.

Goh swept aside opposition attempts to focus voters' minds on the rising cost of living and demands for curbs on the PAP's dominance. The party has ruled Singapore since it became self-governing in 1959.
Political analysts had suggested Goh's authority might be damaged if the poll showed an erosion of support for the PAP.
The ruling party's share of the vote fell steadily from a high of 77.7 percent in 1980 to a low of 61 percent in 1991 just after Goh took over the premiership from Lee Kuan Yew.
But any doubts over Goh's ability to win elections and step out of the shadow of his predecessor have now been dispelled, said Bruce Gale of Political and Economic Risk Consultancy.

"Goh looked very happy last night," he said. "The strong win for the PAP, especially the improvement in the share of the vote and the loss of two opposition seats, put Goh in a strong position in both government and party."
The PAP used every tactic at its disposal to win votes, from a barrage of personal attacks on opposition leaders to promises of extra money for wards with government supporters.
Goh's opening blast was a stern warning to voters that failure to support the PAP would mean losing out on a multi-billion dollar programme to renovate housing estates.
That brought criticism from the U.S. State Department, which Goh accused of interfering in a normal election campaign.
Goh raised the tempo further by staking his personal prestige to a PAP win in the multi-member Cheng San constituency.
He made the pledge midway through the campaign, when straw polls suggested the left-leaning Workers' Party (WP) had a chance of winning five seats in the mainly working-class constituency.

Goh and his two deputy prime ministers Lee Hsien Loong and Tony Tan campaigned in person in Cheng San, accusing one of the WP candidates, Tang Liang Hong, of being a "Chinese chauvinist" who was a danger to the harmony of multi-racial Singapore.
Race is a highly emotive issue in Singapore, which is 77 percent ethnic Chinese with significant Malay and Tamil minorities and suffered bloody race riots in the 1960s.
Goh was jubilant after the last result showed a close win for the PAP in Cheng San.
Both of Singapore's best-known opposition figures, Joshua Jeyaretnam of the Workers' Party and Chee Soon Juan, failed to get into parliament.
Chee, near tears after the end of a campaign in which PAP leaders had branded him a "proven liar", said after his defeat he would take a few weeks off to think over his future.
